title: Messier 72, a celestial city from above
caption: The globular cluster Messier 72, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 72 · constellation Aquarius · about 50000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Scattered stars fill this Hubble image of Messier 72, looking rather like a city seen from an aeroplane window at night, with small glints from suburban homes dotting the outskirts of a bright centre. In reality it is a globular cluster: an ancient ball of old stars that crowd together much more tightly toward the middle, like buildings at a city's heart.

Besides its own huge numbers of stars, the picture also catches many far more distant galaxies, visible between and around the cluster's stars. They are separate systems lying far beyond our galaxy, glimpsed through the gaps.

Pierre Méchain, a French astronomer, found the cluster in August 1780, yet it is named after his colleague Charles Messier, who logged it as the 72nd entry in his catalogue of comet-like objects only two months afterwards. Its home is Aquarius, the Water Bearer, some 50 000 light-years away.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.43 x 3.43 arcminutes) and distance (50000 light years), the frame spans roughly 50 × 50 light-years. Its light set out about 50,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using yellow (F606W) and near-infrared (F814W) filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the distant background galaxies are far too faint to see without a large telescope.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: This was the first image in ESA/Hubble's weekly Picture of the Week series. It was taken with the Advanced Camera for Surveys' Wide Field Channel through yellow and near-infrared filters, with exposures of about ten minutes each, and covers about 3.4 arcminutes.
alt: A rich collection of scattered stars, densest at a bright centre, with faint distant galaxies between and around them.
